source.title: Running Fewer Loops Removes Refusal Behaviour in Recurrent-Depth Language Models
source.authors: Seyedarmin Azizi; Erfan Baghaei Potraghloo; Arya Fayyazi; Saeid Shokoufa; M. Pedram

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Conceptually tests whether a refusal-associated direction causally affects refusal, but its direction is computed as refused-minus-complied rather than harmful-minus-harmless, and its intervention is applied to recurrent-depth models rather than reproducing the original setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own interventions on a refusal direction, probes of harmfulness, and training/depth outcomes relevant to the listed versions. No cited result from another study is recorded as a row. Intermediate-loop direction similarities and the broader depth, attack, judge, and decoding sweeps are not exhaustively tabulated here; key intervention and training results are retained.
record.test_reason: The study builds a refusal direction by difference in means and ablates and adds it in a new setting: recurrent-depth (looped) Ouro models, including reasoning 'Thinking' checkpoints. It reports refusal rates under these edits, with a random-direction control. Two departures from the original: the direction is refused-minus-complied rather than harmful-minus-harmless, and the edit is a hook on the shared normalisation layer. Most of the paper is about loop truncation and depth-aware training, which no version names.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right, but the emphasis is off. The main conclusion is that loop count is a safety setting: fewer loops remove refusal faster than harm detection or task ability, and run-time repairs (exit gates, per-request depth) fail. Training at random depths fixes the problem without over-refusal and with no full-depth cost. The direction results are presented as diagnosis. Harm is readable after one loop, but the refusal direction has not settled. Refusal at full depth depends on that direction: ablation drops Ouro-1.4B's gap from +0.800 to +0.080. The authors also say a fixed added direction is not enough as a repair.
record.recipe_differences: The paper's refusal direction is the difference between mean states on refused and complied prompts, not harmful minus harmless prompts. It applies activation removal/addition through a shared normalisation hook in recurrent-depth models, and also tests loop truncation and depth-aware safety training.
record.method_sensitivity: Direction effects vary by checkpoint: full-depth removal is large on Ouro-1.4B but much smaller on the two reported Thinking checkpoints; one-loop addition changes harmful-versus-harmless separation selectively on Ouro-1.4B-Thinking. Direction alignment with the full-depth direction also varies by model and loop depth. Random-loop versus final-loop training changes shallow-depth refusal separation.

fits_no_version.finding: Running fewer loops in recurrent-depth models removes refusal faster than harm detection or GSM8K ability. The reverse order holds when layers are removed from dense models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In weight-tied looped models, refusal is formed late in depth and is lost first under loop truncation.

fits_no_version.finding: The refusal direction computed after one loop has cosine 0.41–0.84 to the full-depth direction. Earlier settling tracks better retention of refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How early across depth the refusal direction stabilises predicts how robust refusal is to reduced computation.

fits_no_version.finding: Safety training at randomly chosen loop depths keeps the refusal gap at one loop (+0.399 vs +0.118) and Huginn harmful compliance at or below 0.040 across 1–32 loops, with no full-depth GSM8K cost.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Supervising refusal at every depth makes safety robust to inference-depth reduction.

record.problems: The direction interventions are reported for three Ouro checkpoints, with substantial variation across them; no general-capability measure is reported for the direction ablation itself. The direction definition differs from the claim's harmful-minus-harmless definition. The paper notes that it did not repeat safety training with more than one seed per objective, although it does report a three-seed check for the Ouro objective comparison.
record.rows_left_out: Not all intermediate-depth probe and direction-similarity values from Appendix B, Table 7 are listed. Also omitted are the full loop-count safety curves, extensive judge/decoding checks, prompt-template attack sweeps, and additional training comparisons; they are reported in Sections 4–7 and Appendices B, F, H, and I, but are not direct tests of the listed single-direction, transfer, or weight-edit claims. No cited results are included.

untested.parts: Harmful-minus-harmless construction of the direction. Capability after ablation (no GSM8K or other measure under the direction edit). Whether the edit covers all layers and positions. Addition at full depth.
All of V2: no weight-edit or abliteration.
All of V3: jailbreak templates are crossed with depth, but no direction measurement is made under attack and there is no training against ablation.
All of V4: no comparison of multi-direction, cone or affine accounts.
All of V6: no transfer of a direction across languages or models.
Whether training creates a single removable direction. The random-loop versus final-loop training results measure only refusal robustness to depth, not the direction.
Only two Ouro Thinking checkpoints. No other reasoning families, and no intervention during the reasoning trace itself.
No causal intervention on a harmfulness direction separate from the refusal direction.

missing.what: One-loop versus full-depth harmful and harmless refusal rates and refusal gap for each checkpoint. These are needed for the V5 dissociation of harm readability from refusal.
Final-direction AUC at one loop (0.880, 0.887, 0.966) against the depth-fitted probe. This shows harm information is present but not along the full-depth refusal direction.
Separate harmful and harmless refusal rates under one-loop addition on Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B-Thinking. The text says only that both rose similarly.
Harmful compliance rising 0.050→0.850 under ablation on Ouro-1.4B. It is currently only in a note and could be its own row.

record.verdict_notes: The direction is mean(refused) minus mean(complied), applied via a hook on the shared normalisation layer. Positions and layers are not specified. No capability check is made under ablation, and the sample size for the intervention runs is not stated. The intervention baselines (e.g. Ouro-1.4B-Thinking one-loop harmless refusal 0.490, gap -0.170) do not match Table 1 or Table 5, so the edits were probably evaluated on a different subset or protocol. The reader marked V7 as tested, but no direction is measured after training, so those rows go to fits_no_version. The base-versus-Thinking contrast in ablation size (R1 vs R4) could hint at V7, but it is confounded with model size and the authors do not frame it that way. 'Base' Ouro checkpoints already refuse (harmful refusal 0.887 at full depth). Tranche set to T3 because this is a new architecture setting rather than the same method.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not construct the direction as harmful-minus-harmless, does not establish that the edit is applied at every layer and position, and does not measure general capability after direction ablation.
No inference-time direction ablation is converted into a weight edit or evaluated as abliteration.
Jailbreak templates are tested alongside reduced loop counts, but the attacks are not shown to suppress the direction; training is not specifically against direction ablation.
The paper does not compare affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts. It studies one direction and reports variation in its effects across checkpoints.
The paper probes harmful-versus-harmless information and intervenes on a refusal direction, but does not directly measure an independent causal representation of harmfulness judgment.
Different model families and checkpoints are studied, but a direction is not transferred across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Training objectives and depth robustness are compared, but the paper does not directly measure whether training creates or removes a single-direction mechanism in each trained model.
The paper includes Ouro Thinking checkpoints, but does not study other reasoning-model families or separately identify reasoning traces as the cause of any effect.

tranche.reason: It ablates and adds a difference-in-means refusal direction in a new setting (recurrent-depth Ouro), with results on refusal. The direction recipe differs (refused minus complied), but the setting is the main novelty.

source_check.notes: The Section 5.2 intervention numbers come from an unstated evaluation set, with no n, no uncertainty and no capability check under the edit. Its baselines differ from Table 1 (Ouro-1.4B full-depth harmful refusal 0.950 vs 0.887; 1.4B-Thinking one-loop harmless 0.490 vs 0.173). Addition on Ouro-1.4B (gap -0.100->-0.050) and Ouro-2.6B-Thinking (+0.350->+0.370) raised refusal non-selectively, and no row records this.

statements.correction: Ouro-1.4B full-depth ablation: harmful refusal 0.950->0.130, gap +0.800->+0.080, with no uncertainty, no random-direction control (the control was run only for addition) and no capability measure under the edit. GSM8K is measured across depths only. Ouro applies one transformer stack r times (looped, recurrent depth).
statements.problem: The Ouro numbers are right. But the 'why' gives study-level flags (controls, capability, uncertainty) that the cited ablation result does not have. Also, Ouro is a weight-tied dense autoregressive transformer, not outside that class.

statements.correction: One-loop probe AUC: 0.960 / 0.967 / 0.982 (full depth 0.982 / 0.986 / 0.989). Refusal gap retained at one loop: 0.359 (Ouro-1.4B, D +0.737->+0.264), 0.161 (1.4B-Thinking, +0.827->+0.133), 0.555 (2.6B-Thinking, +0.834->+0.463). The forced-choice measure shows no effect on 2.6B-Thinking.
statements.problem: The AUCs are right. '0.359' and '0.555' are fractions of the full-depth gap retained, not gap values. Also, refusal is reduced rather than lost for Ouro-1.4B and Ouro-2.6B-Thinking.

statements.correction: The text calls Ouro-1.4B the base version, as opposed to Thinking, and does not describe its safety training. At full depth its harmful refusal is 0.887 and its gap +0.737 (Table 1).
statements.problem: Ouro-1.4B is the 'base version' only in the sense of not being reasoning-trained. It refuses like a safety-trained model, so R12/R13 don't bear on separation before safety training.
